newsitem.title: INDIA: CRICKET-FROM MHARAJAHS TO MAGNATES, INDIA REFLECTS THE TIMES.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET-FROM MHARAJAHS TO MAGNATES, INDIA REFLECTS THE TIMES.

text.p: From maharajas to magnates, Indian cricket has reflected the temper of the times.
The Indian legacy to the game invented on the English village green was celebrated by an exhibition in the northern Indian state of Punjab during the recent Independence Cup.
The exhibition, in the Punjab Cricket Association's stadium and opened by Sir Garfield Sobers, formed the outline of a planned museum and a cricket library.

It showed replicas of the cricket bat through the ages and displayed the evolution of cricketing clothes from the frilly tops and multi-coloured blazers of the Marylebone Cricket Club (MCC) to more sober latter-day versions.
Alongside was a portrait of Kumar Shri Ranjisinhji, resplendent in a flowing robe and a turban.
Ranji, a maharajah from ancient Rajput stock, played test cricket for England in the late 19th century, bringing a touch of eastern magic to the playing fields of England.
Maharajas were major patrons of cricket in India during colonial rule that ended in 1947.

Five young architects who put together the exhibition drew heavily from the palace archives of the Maharaja of Patiala, Bhupinder Singh, who hosted many visiting English teams during the British Raj and built the game's highest ground some 1,800 metres above sea level in the Himalayan town of Chail.
On display at the show were photographs of MCC players in hunting gear, dating back to the times when visiting cricketers unwound on "shikar" (hunting) expeditions with the local rajahs.
There is also the interesting, if possibly apocryphal anecdote, involving England's Maurice Tate and the Maharaja of Patiala during a match at Lahore between the MCC and Patiala.
Apparently the Maharaja was caught at slip but Tate chose not to appeal.
When asked why by team mate R.E.S. Wyatt, Tate replied: "Don't be a fool. We'll be staying at the chap's palace later on. I don't want to be poisoned."
The exhibition's scrap-book of cricket reports had one titled "India's lessons for Young England" from H.J.Henley, cricket correspondent for the Daily Mail in 1932.
"Among the things shown by the Indians that young England might emulate was the quickness with they went to the wicket," Henley wrote.

Colonial cricket also had its moments of tension. Bombay's Pentangular series between Hindus, Moslems, Christians, Parsees and Europeans was stopped because independence leader Mahatma Gandhi felt it accentuated India's social divides.
A silver bat at the exhibition stood as a witness to the age of the maharajas and emphasised how far the game has come since the days of the princes.
Today's Indian cricketing heroes such as captain Sachin Tendulkar come from more humble stock. And sponsorship is from private companies, not feudal rulers.
Punjab Cricket Association executive Sanjit Sinha said he expected to put all available information on the Internet, to enable access to fans all over the world.
Later this month, India's Jagmohan Dalmiya is scheduled to take over as the new chairman of the International Cricket Council (ICC), the first man from the subcontinent to hold the post.
Last year, Dalmiya turned the World Cup hosted jointly by India, Pakistan and Sri Lanka into a $100-million business event, largely helped by television advertisements.
The construction magnate's plans include a global boost to the game with slick marketing and new rules.
